newsitem.title: MEXICO: Telmex chief Slim says ready to take on rivals.
newsitem.headline: Telmex chief Slim says ready to take on rivals.

text.p: A few short years ago, Mexicans frustrated with phone service viewed Telefonos de Mexico and its billionaire owner Carlos Slim with the kind of annoyance usually reserved for bad tequila and tortillas gone cold.

But things have changed in the years since Slim and a handful of partners took over the former state-run telephone giant in 1990, trimming it down and investing billions of dollars to create a modern phone company more and more Mexicans are proud of.

Once the darling of Wall Street following its 1990 privatization, Telmex has been hurt in the past few years by Mexico's peso crisis and the opening of the country's telephone market to competition, which began on January 1.

Despite Mexico's economic woes, Telmex went on a spending spree in the past few years to get ready for heavyweight rivals such as AT&T and MCI Communications, who have linked up with local partners to beat Telmex.
Telmex spent $500 million in 1996 alone installing a high-tech switching center that would allow rivals to connect to its local network for a fee.
Slim says most Mexicans are now happy enough with Telmex to resist defecting to a host of new rivals competing with the former monopoly for Mexico's lucrative long-distance market.

"Our whole company's attitude has changed...Before, you had to wait months for a new telephone line, now its a matter of days. We digitalized the network and service is better," Slim said in wide-ranging talk Wednesday with a small group of foreign journalists invited to his home.

"We carried out an unprecedented effort to get ready for the competition. They were the ones that weren't ready on time," said Slim, whom Forbes magazine considers Latin America's wealthiest man, worth at least $6 billion.
Most of Telmex's new rivals, including AT&T's Alestra, are heavily dependent on Telmex's network right now, he said.
Slim is confident enough about Telmex's ability that it has already drawn up plans to attack the U.S. market with partner Sprint at the same time that U.S. firms are competing south of the border.
Telmex plans to use Sprint's fiber-optic network to provide long-distance service to the U.S. market's large Hispanic population, which has not traditionally been a target market for U.S. carriers.

He said Telmex could compete in the U.S. market both on service and price, undercutting U.S. carriers' international long-distance prices. "The margins there are high...the risk is low. As you Americans say, the upside is much greater than the downside," he said.

Telmex will likely apply for a license to operate in the U.S. market in the coming weeks, he said. It has already been in talks with the U.S. Federal Communications Commission for more than a year about the opening of the U.S. market.
"What we want is the same access to the U.S. market that U.S. telephone companies have with Mexico," he said.

Slim said competition in Mexico would hurt Telmex's long-distance revenues, which he said would fall in 1997 compared to 1996 and 1995 as rivals won market share and long-distance prices fell. He declined to estimate how much market share Telmex might lose.
But he said overall market growth, newer services like the Internet and the company's plans to tackle the U.S. market should more than make up for market share loss.

"Long distance will become less important anyway as prices continue to fall," he said. He added that Telmex will begin reporting quarterly results for both local and long-distance service for the fourth quarter of last year.
Slim said Telmex's rivals have already begun cutting prices in a bid to capture market share and that prices could fall further still.

"Prices are still at a profitable level for Telmex. But if you are a competitor, and have high fixed costs right now, a small customer base, and an interconnection fee, it's not a good business," he said.
Telmex plans to introduce a single rate of 1.30 pesos per minute on domestic long distance -- similar to that of its competitors.

Telmex CEO Jaime Chico Pardo said the company was pleased with the result of a pre-subscription process in the central city of Queretaro, where residents were able to choose their long-distance carrier ahead of the January 1 opening date.
Telmex won slightly more than 30 percent of the ballots, which were returned by about a third of the city, he said.

Chico Pardo discounted allegations by its rivals that Telmex had held up the pre-subscription process in Queretaro and the northern city of Monterrey. Residents who do not specify another carrier will automatically go to Telmex.

"There were some problems, but it was not a serious delay," he said, adding that Telmex delivered on Wednesday a nationwide database to a U.S. company that will mail out ballots to residents across the nation in the coming months.
Slim said Telmex's rivals were offering inducements in Monterrey, including offering free movie passes and free food for residents who picked up a ballot.
"We are now adopting a similarly aggressive position," he said.
((--Mexico City newsroom, +525 728-9565))
